summary: Johann Gildemeister was an Indologist. He studied at Göttingen under Heinrich Ewald and at Bonn under Georg Freytag, Christian Lassen, and August Wilhelm von Schlegel. He later served as professor at Marburg (1845–1859) and Bonn (1859–1890).

Johann Gottfried Eichhorn worked in religious studies, history, archaeology, and linguistics. He studied at the University of Göttingen under Christian Gottlob Heyne (1770–1774), later becoming a professor at the University of Jena (1775) and Göttingen (1788).

Johann Gottfried Ludwig Kosegarten was an Indologist and linguist. He studied at Greifswald and under Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy, Ernst Moritz Arndt, and Hermann Baier. He served as a professor at Jena (1817–1824) and Greifswald (1824–1850).

Johann Gottfried von Herder worked in philosophy, linguistics, and religious studies. He studied theology at the University of Königsberg in 1761. His career included teaching posts in Riga and serving as director of the Wilhelm-Ernst-Gymnasium Weimar (c. 1776–1803).

Johann Gustav Stickel was a scholar of linguistics. He studied at the University of Jena (1823–1826) under Johann Gottfried Ludwig Kosegarten and later under Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy. He served as a professor at Jena from 1830 to 1836.
Johann II Bernoulli studied at the University of Basel from approximately 1724 to 1729. He later held an academic post at the University of Basel from around 1743 to 1790.

Johann III Bernoulli was active in Indology and history and archaeology. He studied under Daniel Bernoulli at Basel (doctor in philosophy, c. 1757–1758) and Neuchâtel (c. 1758–1760), later holding memberships in the Prussian, Russian, and Danzig scientific academies.
Johann Jakob Engel was a philosopher who studied at the University of Rostock from around 1757 to 1762 and at the University of Leipzig from around 1762 to 1765.

Johann Tobias Beck was a religious studies scholar. He studied at the University of Tübingen from around 1822 to 1826. He later held posts at the University of Basel (c. 1836–1843) and the University of Tübingen (c. 1843–1878).

Johann Wilhelm Andreas Pfaff was an Indologist. He studied at the University of Tübingen (c. 1791–1795) and held posts at the University of Tartu (c. 1803–1809), Würzburg (c. 1814–1818), and Erlangen-Nuremberg (c. 1818–1835).

Johanna Engelberta van Lohuizen-de Leeuw was an archaeologist and Indologist. She studied at Leiden and under Jan Gonda at Utrecht (doctoral degree, c. 1946–1949). She held posts at Cambridge and served as Director of Amsterdam's Institute of South Asian Archaeology (1958–1983).

Johanna Narten was an Indologist, Iranian and Central Asian studies scholar, and linguist. She studied at Saarland under Ernst Zinn and completed her PhD under Karl Hoffmann and habilitation at Erlangen-Nuremberg, where she was an assistant (1973–1977).

Johannes Beltz is a scholar of Indology, religious studies, and Buddhist studies. He completed his doctoral studies by 1999 at the University of Lausanne and the École Pratique des Hautes Études under Johannes Bronkhorst and Marie-Louise Reiniche.

Johannes Bronkhorst is an Indologist, Buddhist studies scholar, and philosopher. He studied at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Rajasthan, Savitribai Phule Pune under S. D. Joshi, and Leiden. He served at Leiden, the Kern Institute, and as professor at Lausanne (1987–2011).

Johannes Gijsbertus de Casparis was an Indologist, historian, and archaeologist. He studied at Leiden University from around 1934 to 1939. He later held posts at SOAS University of London (c. 1964–1981) and as professor at Leiden University (1978–1986).

Johannes Hertel was an Indologist who earned his Dr. phil. at the University of Leipzig (1892–1897). He taught at the Lessing-Gymnasium Döbeln (c. 1898–1920) before holding the chair of Indian philology at Leipzig from 1919 to 1937.

Johannes Klatt was an Indologist who studied under Albrecht Weber and earned a doctorate at the University of Halle-Wittenberg (c. 1869–1873). He worked at the Royal Library of Berlin as staff, assistant, custodian, and librarian between 1872 and 1889.

Johannes Nobel was an Indologist, Tibetologist, and Buddhist studies scholar. He studied at Greifswald and under Heinrich Lüders at Berlin. He worked at the Royal Library of Berlin, Berlin University, and held the Indology chair at Marburg (1928–1955).

Johannes Rahder was a scholar of Indology, Japanology, and Buddhist studies. He earned a doctorate at Utrecht University, where he became a professor in 1930. He held the chair of Japanese at Leiden (1931–1946) and a professorship at Yale (1947–1965).

Johannes Schmidt was a linguist and Indologist. He studied at Bonn, Jena, and under August Schleicher, Albrecht Weber, Friedrich Wilhelm Ritschl, and Otto Jahn. He held professorships at Bonn (1868), Graz (1873–1876), and Berlin (1876).
